The method · after Woods

Six stages, plus a problem record and a review

Each stage asks one question and ends with a deliverable. You move right only when that deliverable exists: facts before causes, tests before fixes.

Part 2

What do you fill at each stage, and where does the OTS feed it?

Part 2 · the plan

From a symptom to a closed case

  1. Stage navigatorevery sub-step and what the OTS gives it
  2. Problem and Engagefacts first, then how urgent it is
  3. Define and Explorea testable statement, then causes you can kill
  4. Plan, Do it, Look backtests, the fix and the barrier
  5. OTS data and evidencethe three live pulls, and the CSV route

Interactive · click a stage

Every sub-step, and what the OTS gives it

Every stage has a source in the OTS; nothing in the workbook is filled from memory.

Problem · Review

Stage 0 records what was seen, not why

The navigator showed where each stage gets its data. Stage 0 comes first, and it only observes.

  • Symptoms with who, when and which tag
  • Normal against now, from the snapshot
  • Pinned trends from the run data
  • A check flags any cause word left in Stage 0

Engage

Is it time-critical: run, safe-park or shut down?

CheckRead it fromDecides
Safety, equipmenttrip limits on the SIS tabminutes left
Production, productFI-108, AI-120cost per hour
Who to tellsupervisor, other units1.7 message

Safe-park: a reduced, stable state that stops the problem growing while you investigate.

Define

A problem statement you can test

  • IS / IS NOT: where it is, and where it could be but is not
  • SMARTS-S target: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, timed, safe
  • 2.11 joins them into one sentence

Explore

Causes you could prove wrong

  • Balances close first (3.2 calculators)
  • Fishbone ideas become working hypotheses (WH): WH-1, WH-2…
  • Each has an if-then and a reading that would kill it
  • Rank by P × S × T: probability, severity, testability

Plan

Screen with S / D / N, then plan the tests

  • Each evidence line Supports, Disproves or is Neutral
  • One solid D kills a hypothesis
  • Tests: one move, a prediction per hypothesis, a stop rule, a way back
  • The cost ledger opens here

Do it · Look back

The workbook judges each test against your prediction

  • Make the move on the OTS, pull the run again
  • Δ (change) after against before, per hypothesis
  • Stage 6: the barrier, the ledger closed, lessons

Example 3.1 · problem statement · read first
EXAMPLE 3.1TE-3 · Wash column pressure climbing

  

    

      
Situation given to you (case sheet)

      
Over the last half hour PI-105 has risen from 6 to almost 10 bar g. The product flow and purity are normal. The feed, TIC-110 and DIC-115 have not been touched.

      
PI-105 is the hydraulic (piston) pressure of the wash column W-104; it trips W-104 at 16 bar g (PSHH-105). Load TE-3, run 30 min without touching anything, then solve it with the six stages and hand in the project file.

Review · the principle
EXAMPLE 3.1A packed crystal bed resists flow

  
The crystals shrank before PI-105 rose. Why would finer crystals raise the pressure?

  

    
$$\frac{\Delta P}{H} = \frac{180\,\mu\,u\,(1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^{3}\,d^{2}}$$

    

      
$\Delta P,\ H$
pressure drop across the bed, bed height
bar, m

      
$\mu$
liquid viscosity in the bed
Pa·s

      
$u$
superficial liquid velocity, grows with the feed
m/s

      
$\varepsilon,\ d$
bed voidage; crystal size (AI-116)
–, µm

    

    
Kozeny–Carman: halve the crystal size and the bed term quadruples.

  






  
Explore · 3.2 from two points
EXAMPLE 3.1Fit PI-105 to the crystal sizestep 1 of 2

  

    
Kozeny–Carman, previous slide$\Delta P \propto 1/d^{2}$

    
$P = a + b\left(\dfrac{250}{L}\right)^{2}$piston and screen part $a$, bed part $b$

    
$5.99 = a + b\,(1.00)$,   $9.63 = a + b\,(1.90)$00:00 at 250 µm; 00:30 at 181 µm

    
$b = \dfrac{3.64}{0.90} = 4.03$,   $a = 1.96$ bar gsubtract the two lines

    
$L$: AI-116 mean size, µm; $a$, $b$: bar g at 250 µm and 40 t/h.

  






  
Interactive · move size and feed
EXAMPLE 3.1Does the bed law reproduce the plant?step 2 of 2

  

    

      
Fitted, previous slide$P = 1.96 + 4.03\left(\dfrac{250}{L}\right)^{2}\dfrac{F}{40}$

      

      

    

    
predicted PI-105, bar g

  

  
At 40 t/h the law hits the plant within 0.1 bar; at 34 t/h it over-predicts by 0.7 bar, so part of $a$ also scales with flow.

Before you leave
Key Takeaways

  

    
1
Record facts in Stage 0; keep every cause for Explore.

    
2
Count the minutes to the trip before you look for the cause.

    
3
Write each hypothesis so one reading could kill it.

    
4
Test with one move and a prediction; let the data judge.

    
5
Close with a barrier and a ledger, then hand in the .woods.json.
